claim: Glycine protects cells against rupture from diverse types of injury, a phenomenon first recognized more than 30 years ago.
source: First recognized more than 30 years ago, glycine protects cells against rupture from diverse types of injury.
evidence: Supported by citation to Weinberg et al., 1987 in the Introduction section

claim: Glycine cytoprotection was first described in 1987 where glycine was found to protect renal tubular cells against hypoxic injury.
source: This cytoprotective effect was first described in 1987, where glycine was found to protect renal tubular cells against hypoxic injury (Weinberg et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weinberg et al., 1987

claim: Similar glycine cytoprotective observations have been replicated across immune, parenchymal, endothelial, and neuronal cell types in multiple injury models.
source: Since, similar observations have been replicated across immune, parenchymal, endothelial, and neuronal cell types in multiple injury models (reviewed in Weinberg et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to review by Weinberg et al., 2016

claim: Glycine protects cells in the lytic cell death pathways pyroptosis and necrosis.
source: These include the lytic cell death pathways pyroptosis (Loomis et al., 2019; Volchuk et al., 2020) and necrosis (Estacion et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Loomis et al., 2019; Volchuk et al., 2020; and Estacion et al., 2003

claim: The molecular target and mechanism by which glycine protects cells and tissues remain elusive.
source: While the robust cytoprotective effects of glycine are widespread, the molecular target and mechanism by which glycine protects cells and tissues remain elusive.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap in the Introduction

claim: Glycine or ATP metabolic pathways have been ruled out as underlying the glycine cytoprotection phenomenon.
source: These include glycine or ATP metabolic pathways (Weinberg et al., 1991), intracellular calcium or pH regulation (Weinberg et al., 1994), cytoskeleton stabilization (Chen et al., 1997), and chloride conductance (Loomis et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Weinberg et al., 1991

claim: Intracellular calcium or pH regulation have been ruled out as underlying the glycine cytoprotection phenomenon.
source: These include glycine or ATP metabolic pathways (Weinberg et al., 1991), intracellular calcium or pH regulation (Weinberg et al., 1994), cytoskeleton stabilization (Chen et al., 1997), and chloride conductance (Loomis et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weinberg et al., 1994

claim: Cytoskeleton stabilization has been ruled out as underlying the glycine cytoprotection phenomenon.
source: These include glycine or ATP metabolic pathways (Weinberg et al., 1991), intracellular calcium or pH regulation (Weinberg et al., 1994), cytoskeleton stabilization (Chen et al., 1997), and chloride conductance (Loomis et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 1997

claim: Chloride conductance has been ruled out as underlying the glycine cytoprotection phenomenon.
source: These include glycine or ATP metabolic pathways (Weinberg et al., 1991), intracellular calcium or pH regulation (Weinberg et al., 1994), cytoskeleton stabilization (Chen et al., 1997), and chloride conductance (Loomis et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Loomis et al., 2019

claim: It has been speculated that glycine targets a membrane receptor but is unlikely to involve canonical glycine receptors.
source: It has been speculated that glycine targets a membrane receptor but is unlikely to involve canonical glycine receptors (Loomis et al., 2019; Weinberg et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Loomis et al., 2019 and Weinberg et al., 2016

claim: Glycine has oftentimes been described as an osmoprotectant.
source: Lastly, as a cytoprotective agent, glycine has oftentimes been described as an osmoprotectant (Fink and Cookson, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fink and Cookson, 2006

claim: Gasdermin D pores formed during pyroptosis allow transport of small proteins and ions across lipid bilayers.
source: However, its small size should generally allow free passage through the large membrane conduits involved in lytic cell death pathways, such as the gasdermin D pores formed during pyroptosis that are known to allow transport of small proteins and ions across lipid bilayers (Evavold et al., 2018; Heilig et al., 2018; Xia et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Evavold et al., 2018; Heilig et al., 2018; Xia et al., 2021

claim: It remains unknown whether glycine's cytoprotective effect is through an extracellular or intracellular mode of action.
source: Moreover, it remains unknown whether glycine's cytoprotective effect is through an extracellular or intracellular mode of action and, therefore, whether glycine's entry into the cell is required for cytoprotection.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap in the Introduction

claim: NINJ1 was recently identified as the common executioner of plasma membrane rupture in pyroptosis, necrosis, and post-apoptosis lysis.
source: Notably, the transmembrane protein ninjurin-1 (NINJ1) was recently identified as the common executioner of plasma membrane rupture in pyroptosis, necrosis, and post-apoptosis lysis (Kayagaki et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2021

claim: Post-apoptosis lysis refers to the cell membrane rupture that occurs when phagocytes are unable to scavenge apoptotic cells that have otherwise completed the apoptotic program.
source: Post-apoptosis lysis refers to the cell membrane rupture that occurs when phagocytes are unable to scavenge apoptotic cells that have otherwise completed the apoptotic program (Silva, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Silva, 2010

claim: NINJ1 is a 16 kilodalton protein with two transmembrane regions that reside in the plasma membrane.
source: NINJ1 is a 16 kilodalton protein with two transmembrane regions that reside in the plasma membrane with prior reports, suggesting a function in cell adhesion (Araki et al., 1997; Araki and Milbrandt, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Araki et al., 1997 and Araki and Milbrandt, 1996

claim: Prior reports suggest NINJ1 has a function in cell adhesion.
source: NINJ1 is a 16 kilodalton protein with two transmembrane regions that reside in the plasma membrane with prior reports, suggesting a function in cell adhesion (Araki et al., 1997; Araki and Milbrandt, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Araki et al., 1997 and Araki and Milbrandt, 1996

claim: NINJ1 has been implicated in multiple inflammatory conditions, such as nerve injury, atherosclerosis, ischemic brain injury, and tumorigenesis.
source: NINJ1 has been implicated in multiple inflammatory conditions, such as nerve injury, atherosclerosis, ischemic brain injury, and tumorigenesis (Araki and Milbrandt, 1996; Jeon et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Araki and Milbrandt, 1996; Jeon et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2017

claim: The mechanism by which NINJ1 mediates lytic cell death coincides with its clustering within the plasma membrane.
source: The mechanism by which NINJ1 mediates lytic cell death coincides with its clustering within the plasma membrane, and this multimerization is required for membrane disruption by an unknown mechanism (Kayagaki et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2021

claim: NINJ1 multimerization is required for membrane disruption by an unknown mechanism.
source: The mechanism by which NINJ1 mediates lytic cell death coincides with its clustering within the plasma membrane, and this multimerization is required for membrane disruption by an unknown mechanism (Kayagaki et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2021

claim: NINJ1 knockout and glycine treatment protect cells against a common set of lytic cell death pathways.
source: The published literature suggests a potential association between NINJ1 and glycine given that NINJ1 knockout and glycine treatment protect cells against a common set of lytic cell death pathways.
evidence: Based on inference from published literature as stated in the text

claim: In pyroptosis, both NINJ1 knockout and glycine treatment allow for IL-1β secretion through the gasdermin D pore while preventing final membrane lysis.
source: Moreover, in pyroptosis, both allow for IL-1β secretion through the gasdermin D pore while preventing final membrane lysis (Kayagaki et al., 2021; Volchuk et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kayagaki et al., 2021 and Volchuk et al., 2020

claim: NINJ1 knockout in iBMDM protects against pyroptotic cytotoxicity as measured by LDH release.
source: Pyroptosis was induced in LPS(lipopolysaccharide)-primed wildtype and NINJ1 knockout iBMDM with nigericin (20 µM, 2 hr) in the absence or presence of 5 mM glycine. Glycine treatment at 5 mM was based on the reported literature (Loomis et al., 2019; Volchuk et al., 2020) and a dose-finding study (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). We performed a colorimetric assay to test for LDH release, a common marker of cell rupture. Both NINJ1 knockout and glycine treatment in wildtype iBMDM protected against cytotoxicity (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citations to Loomis et al., 2019 and Volchuk et al., 2020

claim: Glycine treatment at 5 mM protects wildtype iBMDM against pyroptotic cytotoxicity as measured by LDH release.
source: Pyroptosis was induced in LPS(lipopolysaccharide)-primed wildtype and NINJ1 knockout iBMDM with nigericin (20 µM, 2 hr) in the absence or presence of 5 mM glycine. Glycine treatment at 5 mM was based on the reported literature (Loomis et al., 2019; Volchuk et al., 2020) and a dose-finding study (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). We performed a colorimetric assay to test for LDH release, a common marker of cell rupture. Both NINJ1 knockout and glycine treatment in wildtype iBMDM protected against cytotoxicity (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citations to Loomis et al., 2019 and Volchuk et al., 2020

claim: NINJ1 knockout and glycine treatment preserve cell membrane integrity following apoptosis induced with venetoclax.
source: Similarly, cell membrane integrity was preserved following apoptosis (Figure 1C) and necrosis (Figure 1D) induced with venetoclax (25 µM, 16 hr) and pneumolysin (0.5 µg/mL, 15 min), respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: NINJ1 knockout and glycine treatment preserve cell membrane integrity following necrosis induced with pneumolysin.
source: Similarly, cell membrane integrity was preserved following apoptosis (Figure 1C) and necrosis (Figure 1D) induced with venetoclax (25 µM, 16 hr) and pneumolysin (0.5 µg/mL, 15 min), respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: In NINJ1 knockout macrophages, treatment with glycine during lytic cell death does not confer any additional protection against cell lysis.
source: Importantly, in NINJ1 knockout macrophages, treatment with glycine during lytic cell death did not confer any additional protection against cell lysis, suggesting that these distinct perturbations affect the same process (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B-D

claim: LPS-primed wildtype iBMDM induced to undergo pyroptosis in the presence of glycine demonstrate similar plasma membrane ballooning to NINJ1 knockout iBMDM induced to undergo pyroptosis.
source: When visualizing glycine-treated pyroptotic macrophages, we observed prominent plasma membrane ballooning (Figure 1E). This impressive morphology was comparable to that of LPS-primed NINJ1 knockout macrophages stimulated to undergo pyroptosis with nigericin, which we (Figure 1E) and others (Kayagaki et al., 2021) have observed.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and citation to Kayagaki et al., 2021

claim: Glycine dose-dependently inhibits rupture of pyroptotic mouse BMDM with an IC50 between 1 and 2 mM.
source: Glycine dose-dependently inhibits rupture of pyroptotic mouse BMDM with an IC50 between 1 and 2 mM, consistent with the published literature (Loomis et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citation to Loomis et al., 2019

claim: Glycine confers greater cytoprotection compared with alanine, serine, and valine as measured by LDH release.
source: Glycine confers greater cytoprotection compared with alanine >> serine, valine as measured by LDH release.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Amino acid treatment limits NINJ1 aggregation in pyroptosis with a hierarchy of glycine > alanine > serine, valine.
source: BN-PAGE for NINJ1 shows that amino acid treatment limits NINJ1 aggregation in pyroptosis with a similar hierarchy of glycine > alanine > serine, valine.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: NINJ1 deficiency in RAW-ASC macrophages functionally phenocopies glycine treatment in pyroptosis as measured by LDH release.
source: To further corroborate the above findings, we conducted pyroptosis assays in RAW mouse macrophages reconstituted with the inflammasome adaptor ASC (hereafter referred to as RAW-ASC). NINJ1 protein expression was ablated through CRISPR-Cas9 targeting as compared with the parental line (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A). Pyroptosis stimulation in this orthogonal murine macrophage model demonstrates NINJ1 deficiency functionally (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and morphologically (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) phenocopies glycine treatment as was seen in the iBMDM system.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: NINJ1 deficiency in RAW-ASC macrophages morphologically phenocopies glycine treatment in pyroptosis.
source: To further corroborate the above findings, we conducted pyroptosis assays in RAW mouse macrophages reconstituted with the inflammasome adaptor ASC (hereafter referred to as RAW-ASC). NINJ1 protein expression was ablated through CRISPR-Cas9 targeting as compared with the parental line (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A). Pyroptosis stimulation in this orthogonal murine macrophage model demonstrates NINJ1 deficiency functionally (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and morphologically (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) phenocopies glycine treatment as was seen in the iBMDM system.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: Native-PAGE analysis of endogenous NINJ1 in RAW-ASC macrophages demonstrates a shift to high molecular weight aggregate upon pyroptosis stimulation, which is abrogated by glycine treatment.
source: Native-PAGE analysis of endogenous NINJ1 in RAW-ASC macrophages demonstrates a shift to high molecular weight aggregate upon pyroptosis stimulation, which is abrogated by glycine treatment.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D

claim: Human NINJ1 is 90% homologous to the mouse protein.
source: Human NINJ1 is 90% homologous to the mouse protein and was shown to be toxic when overexpressed in HEK293T cells (Kayagaki et al., 2021), but it is not known if endogenous NINJ1 is activated and mediates plasma membrane rupture in human cells undergoing programmed cell death.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2021

claim: Human NINJ1 was shown to be toxic when overexpressed in HEK293T cells.
source: Human NINJ1 is 90% homologous to the mouse protein and was shown to be toxic when overexpressed in HEK293T cells (Kayagaki et al., 2021), but it is not known if endogenous NINJ1 is activated and mediates plasma membrane rupture in human cells undergoing programmed cell death.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2021

claim: It is not known if endogenous NINJ1 is activated and mediates plasma membrane rupture in human cells undergoing programmed cell death.
source: Human NINJ1 is 90% homologous to the mouse protein and was shown to be toxic when overexpressed in HEK293T cells (Kayagaki et al., 2021), but it is not known if endogenous NINJ1 is activated and mediates plasma membrane rupture in human cells undergoing programmed cell death.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap in the text

claim: NINJ1 knockdown in primary human monocyte-derived macrophages prevents pyroptosis-induced LDH release.
source: We knocked down NINJ1 in primary human monocyte-derived macrophages (hMDMs) using siRNA specific to NINJ1 (siNINJ1) and compared to non-targeting control siRNA (siCtrl) with an efficiency approaching 70% (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A). Both NINJ1 knockdown and glycine (50 mM; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) independently and completely prevented pyroptosis (LDH release) induced by nigericin (20 µM, 2 hr) in LPS-primed hMDMs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: Glycine at 50 mM prevents pyroptosis-induced LDH release in primary human monocyte-derived macrophages.
source: We knocked down NINJ1 in primary human monocyte-derived macrophages (hMDMs) using siRNA specific to NINJ1 (siNINJ1) and compared to non-targeting control siRNA (siCtrl) with an efficiency approaching 70% (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A). Both NINJ1 knockdown and glycine (50 mM; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) independently and completely prevented pyroptosis (LDH release) induced by nigericin (20 µM, 2 hr) in LPS-primed hMDMs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: There is no additional effect with combined NINJ1 deficiency and glycine treatment in human macrophages undergoing pyroptosis, arguing that NINJ1 and glycine are involved in the same process.
source: Notably, again there was no additional effect with combined NINJ1 deficiency and glycine treatment arguing that NINJ1 and glycine are involved in the same process in primary human cell death pathways (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Human macrophages induced to undergo necroptosis are unprotected by glycine treatment.
source: In contrast, human macrophages induced to undergo necroptosis (zVAD 20 µM + SMAC mimetic BV6 10 µM followed by TNF 10 ng/mL) were unprotected by glycine treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with the observation that Ninj1 knockout does not confer protection in necroptosis likely due to sufficient cytolytic activity of MLKL pores (Kayagaki et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citation to Kayagaki et al., 2021

claim: Ninj1 knockout does not confer protection in necroptosis likely due to sufficient cytolytic activity of MLKL pores.
source: In contrast, human macrophages induced to undergo necroptosis (zVAD 20 µM + SMAC mimetic BV6 10 µM followed by TNF 10 ng/mL) were unprotected by glycine treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with the observation that Ninj1 knockout does not confer protection in necroptosis likely due to sufficient cytolytic activity of MLKL pores (Kayagaki et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2021

claim: Both siNINJ1 and glycine sustain the ballooned morphology of pyroptotic human monocyte-derived macrophages.
source: Like mouse macrophages, both siNINJ1 and glycine sustained the ballooned morphology of pyroptotic hMDMs (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Pyroptotic human macrophages maintained their plasma membrane integrity in the presence of glycine but lost viability as measured by the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and cellular ATP content.
source: While pyroptotic human macrophages maintained their plasma membrane integrity in the presence of glycine as demonstrated by suppressed LDH release, we next confirmed that they had nevertheless lost viability as measured by the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and cellular ATP content (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: The working model of NINJ1-mediated membrane rupture involves its clustering within the plasma membrane.
source: We therefore next posited that glycine targets NINJ1 as part of its cytoprotective effect. The working model of NINJ1-mediated membrane rupture involves its clustering within the plasma membrane (Kayagaki et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2021

claim: Point mutants (e.g. K45Q and A59P) that prevent membrane rupture also fail to cluster upon induction of pyroptosis.
source: Point mutants (e.g. K45Q and A59P) that prevent membrane rupture also fail to cluster upon induction of pyroptosis (Kayagaki et al., 2021), further reinforcing a connection between the clustering process and the capacity of NINJ1 to rupture membranes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2021

claim: Endogenous NINJ1 of otherwise untreated primary mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages migrates at approximately 40 kDa by native-PAGE, potentially indicative of NINJ1 dimers or trimers in unstimulated cells.
source: Using a biochemical native-PAGE approach that maintains native protein interactions, endogenous NINJ1 of otherwise untreated primary mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDM) migrates at approximately 40 kDa, potentially indicative of NINJ1 dimers or trimers in unstimulated cells (Figure 3A) and consistent with its known ability to form homotypic interactions (Bae et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and citation to Bae et al., 2017

claim: A band of approximately 160–200 kDa is observed by native-PAGE in the basal state, suggesting that higher-order multimers of NINJ1 consistent with decamers or higher-order multimers may be present in the plasma membrane of unstimulated macrophages.
source: By native-PAGE, a band of approximately 160–200 kDa is also observed in the basal state, suggesting that higher-order multimers of NINJ1 consistent with decamers or higher-order multimers may also be present in the plasma membrane of unstimulated macrophages (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: In response to pyroptosis, necrosis, and apoptosis induction in primary BMDM, the endogenous NINJ1 signal shifts to a high molecular weight aggregate, suggestive of a clustering process.
source: In response to pyroptosis (nigericin in LPS-primed BMDM), necrosis (pneumolysin), and apoptosis (venetoclax) induction in primary BMDM, the endogenous NINJ1 signal shifts to a high molecular weight aggregate, suggestive of a clustering process.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Glycine treatment abrogates the shift of endogenous NINJ1 to a high molecular weight aggregate in pyroptosis, necrosis, and apoptosis.
source: In response to pyroptosis (nigericin in LPS-primed BMDM), necrosis (pneumolysin), and apoptosis (venetoclax) induction in primary BMDM, the endogenous NINJ1 signal shifts to a high molecular weight aggregate, suggestive of a clustering process. Importantly, this shift is completely abrogated by glycine treatment (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Glycine treatment of primary hMDMs undergoing pyroptosis prevents the shift of NINJ1 to a high molecular weight band by native-PAGE.
source: Using this same native-PAGE approach, glycine treatment of primary hMDMs (Figure 4A) and mouse RAW-ASC cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) undergoing pyroptosis prevented the shift of NINJ1 to a high molecular weight band.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Glycine inhibits NINJ1 oligomerization and pyroptotic lysis in LPS-primed and nigericin-treated human macrophages derived from induced pluripotent stem cells without impairing secretion of IL-1β.
source: Finally, glycine inhibited NINJ1 oligomerization and pyroptotic lysis (as measured by LDH release) in LPS-primed and nigericin-treated human macrophages derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived macrophages (iPSDMs) without impairing secretion of IL-1β, confirming previous findings that glycine acts downstream of GSDMD pore formation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D

claim: Endogenous NINJ1 resides in discrete puncta within the plasma membrane of LPS-primed primary BMDM as observed by total internal reflection microscopy.
source: To corroborate these biochemical findings, we proceeded to evaluate native NINJ1 oligomerization within the plasma membrane by total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy in primary BMDM and hMDMs induced to undergo pyroptosis. TIRF microscopy allows for the preferential excitation of a thin (~150 nm) layer that includes the ventral plasma membrane of adherent cells, thereby eliminating background fluorescence from structures outside this focal plane (e.g. endomembrane compartments). In LPS-primed BMDMs and hMDMs, NINJ1 appears in discrete, small puncta that are diffusely distributed across the plasma membrane in both cell types (Figure 3B, Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Upon induction of pyroptosis, the density of NINJ1 puncta decreases and their intensity increases, consistent with the clustering or aggregation of the low-order multimers into high-order oligomers.
source: Upon induction of pyroptosis, the density of these puncta decreases, and their intensity increases (Figure 3C–D, Figure 4C–D), consistent with the clustering or aggregation of the low-order multimers into high-order oligomers as seen on the native PAGE (Figure 3A, Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3C-D, 4C-D, 3A, and 4A

claim: Co-treatment with glycine abrogates the formation of NINJ1 clusters in pyroptosis as observed by TIRF microscopy.
source: Co-treatment with glycine abrogates the formation of these clusters (Figure 3B–D, Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B-D and 4B-D

claim: STED microscopy improved resolution from a full-width half-maximum by confocal microscopy of 271±98 nm to 63±8 nm.
source: To partially overcome this limitation, we next probed NINJ1 membrane clustering using stimulated emission depletion (STED), a super-resolution fluorescence microscopy approach, in primary BMDM. With STED, we improved upon the resolution from a full-width half-maximum by confocal microscopy of 271±98 nm to 63±8 nm (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: In the basal state, NINJ1 was observed in small discrete puncta by STED microscopy, which decreased in density and increased in intensity upon pyroptosis induction with nigericin.
source: In the basal state, NINJ1 was observed in small discrete puncta, which decreased in density (Figure 3F) and increased in intensity (Figure 3G) upon pyroptosis induction with nigericin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3F and 3G

claim: Co-treatment with glycine (5 mM) limited NINJ1 clustering in pyroptosis as observed by STED microscopy.
source: Co-treatment with glycine (5 mM) limited clustering (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3F-G

claim: Co-treatment with glycine has no effect on caspase-1 activation, GSDMD processing, and IL-1β processing and secretion in iBMDM induced with nigericin.
source: Thus far, our data do not rule out the possibility that glycine is able to target proteins upstream of NINJ1 in pyroptosis. To test whether this is indeed the case, we evaluated caspase-1 activation, GSDMD processing, and IL-1β processing and secretion in iBMDM induced with nigericin with and without 5 mM glycine. Co-treatment with glycine had no effect on these upstream processes (Figure 5A–B), supporting the hypothesis that the target of glycine is downstream and independent of GSDMD activation and oligomerization.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A-B

claim: Glycine dose-dependently suppresses NINJ1-mediated cell rupture independent of activation of upstream programmed cell death pathway activation.
source: To confirm that glycine interferes with NINJ1-mediated cellular rupture independent of upstream signaling pathways, we generated a doxycycline-inducible NINJ1 overexpression system in mouse macrophages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) based on the rationale that sufficient overexpression of NINJ1 can drive spontaneous lysis as seen in 293T systems (Kayagaki et al., 2021). Using this cell-based system, we demonstrate that glycine dose-dependently suppresses NINJ1-mediated cell rupture independent of activation of upstream programmed cell death pathway activation (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and citation to Kayagaki et al., 2021

claim: Expression of N-terminal GSDMD using an inducible system triggers a glycine-inhibitable cellular rupture.
source: Expression of N-terminal GSDMD using a similar inducible system was able to trigger a glycine-inhibitable cellular rupture (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Glycine suppresses NINJ1 clustering when NINJ1 is overexpressed.
source: To further address glycine's mode of action, we evaluated glycine's effect on NINJ1 clustering biochemically and found that glycine suppresses NINJ1 clustering when NINJ1 is overexpressed (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Circular dichroism of the NINJ1 α-helix at varying glycine concentrations between 0 and 20 mM did not affect the CD spectrum, indicating that glycine did not alter the stability of the helical secondary structure.
source: We next turned our attention to the purported amphipathic α-helix in the NINJ1 N-terminus (residues 40–69 of human NINJ1), which others have shown to be necessary for NINJ1-mediated plasma membrane rupture (Kayagaki et al., 2021). Circular dichroism (CD) of the α-helix at varying glycine concentrations between 0 and 20 mM did not affect the CD spectrum, indicating that at the trialed concentrations, glycine did not alter the stability of the helical secondary structure of this region of the NINJ1 N-terminus (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and citation to Kayagaki et al., 2021

claim: The NINJ1 α-helix was able to rupture liposomes, but glycine did not interfere with this effect.
source: We then functionally evaluated whether glycine interferes with the membrane lytic function of the helix using a reconstituted liposomal rupture assay. In this system, we demonstrate that while the α-helix was able to rupture liposomes, glycine did not interfere with this effect (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F

claim: Glycine can block full-length NINJ1 clustering and membrane rupture in cellulo but additional unknown players may be affected within cells, or the mode of action is separate from the minimally sufficient lytic α-helix of the NINJ1 N-terminus.
source: These data suggest that glycine can block full-length NINJ1 clustering and membrane rupture in cellulo but that additional unknown players may be affected within cells, or the mode of action is separate from the minimally sufficient lytic α-helix of the NINJ1 N-terminus as shown by intact liposome rupture.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data on liposome rupture and cellular studies

claim: Glycine treatment and genetic ablation or silencing of NINJ1 yield similar functional and morphological outcomes in both human and mouse macrophages subjected to lytic cell death programs.
source: Our data demonstrate that glycine treatment and genetic ablation or silencing of NINJ1 yield similar functional and morphological outcomes in both human and mouse macrophages subjected to lytic cell death programs.
evidence: Summary statement based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript

claim: Glycine cytoprotection results from interference with NINJ1 clustering within the plasma membrane.
source: Mechanistically, our data suggest that glycine cytoprotection results from interference with NINJ1 clustering within the plasma membrane.
evidence: Summary statement based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript

claim: The mechanism by which glycine interferes with NINJ1 clustering can be either direct or indirect.
source: The mechanism by which glycine interferes with NINJ1 clustering can be either direct or indirect.
evidence: Stated as a possibility in the Discussion

claim: Glycine does not interfere with the secondary structure or lytic function of the NINJ1 α-helix based on in vitro CD studies and liposomal rupture system.
source: Our in vitro CD studies and liposomal rupture system, respectively, indicate that glycine does not interfere with the secondary structure or lytic function of the NINJ1 α-helix.
evidence: Based on experimental data from CD studies and liposomal rupture assays

claim: It remains plausible that glycine interacts directly with the NINJ1 α-helix domain or other components of the NINJ1 N-terminus in cells to interfere with NINJ1 clustering.
source: It remains plausible that glycine still interacts directly with this domain or other components of the NINJ1 N-terminus in cells to interfere with NINJ1 clustering, consistent with our presented data.
evidence: Stated as a possibility in the Discussion

claim: Glycine may act on an unidentified intermediate that modulates NINJ1 clustering within the plasma membrane.
source: Alternatively, glycine may act on an unidentified intermediate that modulates NINJ1 clustering within the plasma membrane.
evidence: Stated as a possibility in the Discussion

claim: In pyroptotic cells, an intermediate between active GSDMD and NINJ1 could be the target of glycine.
source: Our data in pyroptotic cells suggest that such an intermediate would reside between active GSDMD and NINJ1.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing glycine does not affect GSDMD processing

claim: It remains unclear whether glycine's cytoprotective activity occurs on the intracellular or extracellular side of the plasma membrane.
source: In addition, it remains unclear whether glycine's cytoprotective activity occurs on the intracellular or extracellular side of the plasma membrane.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap in the Discussion

claim: There is no direct evidence to suggest whether glycine's cytoprotective effect is specifically mediated from the intracellular or extracellular side.
source: To the best of our knowledge, there is no direct evidence to suggest whether glycine's cytoprotective effect is specifically mediated from the intracellular or extracellular side.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap in the Discussion

claim: Both extracellular and intracellular sites of action for glycine have been proposed.
source: Both extracellular (Weinberg et al., 2016) and intracellular (Rühl and Broz, 2022) sites of action have been proposed.
evidence: Supported by citations to Weinberg et al., 2016 and Rühl and Broz, 2022
